a: the main point
t: The main point, or the sum
p: The Greek can mean the crowning point or a summary of everything said so far.
b: The word is kephalaion, from kephalē, 'head'. It was used for the sum of a column of figures and for the chief point of an argument. Here the writer gathers up chapters 5 to 7 (a priest after the pattern of Melchizedek, appointed by an oath, who lives forever) and turns to what that priest does and where he does it. Chapters 8 to 10 are the center of the sermon.

a: He took his seat at the right hand
p: Psalm 110:1 again: the priest has sat down, which no priest in the tent ever did.
b: Hebrews comes back to Psalm 110:1 again and again (1:3, 13; 8:1; 10:12; 12:2). The site renders the psalm "Sit at my right hand, / until I set your enemies down / as a stool for your feet" (Psalm 110:1). The writer will press the point in 10:11-12: the priests of the tent always stand, because their work is never done, while this priest sits. 'The Majesty' is a reverent way of saying God without the name, as in 1:3.

a: the true tent
t: Tent, the word for the tabernacle
p: Skēnē is the Greek for any tent and for Israel's tabernacle; this site writes 'tent' every time.
b: Skēnē is the Septuagint's usual word for the tabernacle that Moses built (the Septuagint is the Greek translation of the Old Testament made before Jesus). Many Bibles write 'tabernacle', which sounds like a special building; the Greek is the plain word for a tent, the same word used for the tents Abraham lived in (11:9). John 1:14 uses the verb: the Word "pitched his tent among us" (John 1:14). 'True' (alēthinos) means real, the original, not 'honest': the tent Moses built was a copy (8:5; 9:24).

a: minister of the sanctuary
p: Ta hagia, 'the holy things/places', is Hebrews' word for the inner sanctuary where God is met.
b: Hebrews uses the neuter plural ta hagia for the sanctuary, and especially for the innermost room where the high priest went on the Day of Atonement (9:8, 12, 24-25; 10:19; 13:11). Here the sanctuary is in heaven. 'Minister' (leitourgos) is the word for someone who performs a public, sacred service; English 'liturgy' comes from it. In 9:2-3 the writer uses Hagia and Hagia Hagiōn as the names of the two rooms, 'the holy place' and 'the most holy place', as Exodus 26:33 does.

a: On earth he would not even be a priest
p: Jesus was from Judah, not Levi, so in the earthly Temple he had no right to serve.
b: The point was made in 7:13-14: Jesus came from the tribe of Judah, and the Law gave the priesthood to Levi. Hebrews does not argue that Jesus served as a priest in Jerusalem; it argues the opposite. His priesthood belongs to another order and another sanctuary. The present tense ('priests are already there offering') is one of the clues in the debate about whether Hebrews was written before the Temple fell in AD 70 (see the chapter page).

a: a copy and a shadow
p: Hypodeigma and skia: the earthly tent shows the heavenly reality the way a copy or a shadow shows its original.
b: Hypodeigma usually means an example or a sample to imitate; here it is a copy made after a model. Skia is a shadow, cast by something real. Paul uses the same picture: "These are the shadow of what is to come, but the body is Christ's" (Colossians 2:17). Hebrews returns to it in 10:1, where the law has "a shadow of the good things to come, not the actual image". Readers debate whether the background is Plato's world of forms (through Philo of Alexandria) or Jewish teaching about a sanctuary in heaven: see the chapter page.

a: by the pattern you were shown on the mountain
p: Exodus 25:40, in the Greek form, with 'everything' added.
b: The site renders the Hebrew of Exodus 25:40: "See to it that you make them by their pattern, the one you are being shown on the mountain" (Exodus 25:40). The Greek (Swete's Septuagint) uses typos, 'pattern', the word Hebrews keeps here. Hebrews adds 'everything' (panta), which widens the command from the lampstand to the whole tent. Stephen makes the same point in Acts: the tent was built "following the model Moses had seen" (Acts 7:44).

a: was warned by God
p: Chrēmatizō: to receive a word from God, a divine warning or instruction.
b: The same verb is used of Noah, 'given warning about things no one could see yet' (11:7), and of God who 'gave them warning on earth' (12:25). The Plain English Translation uses 'warn' in all three places so the reader can hear the thread: God speaks from heaven, and the hearers must act on what they cannot yet see.

a: better
p: Kreittōn, 'better', runs through Hebrews; the Plain English Translation keeps the one word every time.
b: Hebrews uses kreittōn more than the rest of the New Testament: a better name (1:4), better things (6:9), a better hope (7:19), a better covenant (7:22; 8:6), better promises (8:6), better sacrifices (9:23), a better possession (10:34), a better country (11:16), a better resurrection (11:35), something better for us (11:40), blood that speaks better (12:24). The comparison is always with something good. The argument is 'how much more', not 'bad against good'.

a: mediator
p: Mesitēs: the go-between who brings two parties together and guarantees an agreement.
b: In Greek law a mesitēs was a middleman or guarantor. Paul uses the word of Moses at Sinai (Galatians 3:19-20) and of Christ: "one also is the mediator between God and humans: Christ Jesus, himself human" (1 Timothy 2:5). Hebrews uses it three times, always with the new covenant (8:6; 9:15; 12:24). In 7:22 Jesus is the 'guarantor' (engyos) of a better covenant.

a: made law
p: Nenomothetētai: the new covenant has been legally enacted, with the same verb used of the Law in 7:11.
b: The verb nomotheteō means to lay down as law. In 7:11 the people 'received the law' on the basis of the Levitical priesthood; here the new covenant has been enacted on better promises. The writer does not set law against no law: he sets one legally founded covenant against another. The promises are those of Jeremiah 31, quoted next.

a: Look, days are coming, says the Lord
p: Hebrews quotes Jeremiah 31:31-34 in full from the Greek, then returns to it in 10:16-17.
b: The Hebrew is Jeremiah 31:31-34; in the Greek Jeremiah it is chapter 38, verses 31-34, because the Greek book is ordered differently. The site renders the Hebrew: "Look, days are coming, the LORD declares, when I will cut a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah" (Jeremiah 31:31). Hebrews follows the Greek closely, with small changes: 'I will bring to completion' (syntelesō) where Swete's Septuagint has 'I will arrange' (diathēsomai), and 'says' (legei) for 'declares' (phēsin). 'Lord' stands for the divine name, as everywhere in the Greek Old Testament.

a: I for my part neglected them
t: 'I neglected them' or 'I was their husband'?
p: Hebrews and the Septuagint read 'I neglected them'; the Hebrew Masoretic text says 'though I had married them'.
b: Hebrews has the same words as the Septuagint: kai egō ēmelēsa autōn, 'and I for my part neglected them' (in Swete's edition, mainly Codex Vaticanus; Jeremiah 38:32 in the Greek numbering). The Hebrew has ve'anokhi ba'alti vam, which the site renders "though I had married them" (Jeremiah 31:32). Scholars explain the difference in more than one way, from the way the translators read the Hebrew verb to the way they understood it. Hebrews' version gives the warning a sharper edge: when the people left the covenant, God let them go.

a: I will put my laws into their minds
t: The law written on the heart
p: The heart of Jeremiah's promise: God's law inside people, not only on stone.
b: The site renders the Hebrew: "I will put my law inside them, and on their hearts I will write it. I will be their God, and they will be my people" (Jeremiah 31:33). Hebrews' Greek has the plural 'laws' (nomous) where the Hebrew has 'law'. It has 'mind' in the singular (tēn dianoian autōn, 'their mind', one mind for the whole people) and 'hearts' in the plural; the Plain English Translation writes 'minds' because English needs the plural for many people. In 10:16 the Byzantine text has the plural 'minds' (dianoiōn). Ezekiel promises the same with a new heart and spirit (Ezekiel 36:26-27), and Paul draws on it when he calls the Corinthians a letter written "on tablets that are hearts of flesh" (2 Corinthians 3:3). The promise does not say the law is abolished; it says where it will be written.
orig: διδοὺς νόμους μου εἰς τὴν διάνοιαν αὐτῶν (didous nomous mou eis tēn dianoian autōn)

a: I will never again remember their sins
p: God 'not remembering' sins is a picture of forgiveness, not a gap in God's knowledge.
b: In the Bible to 'remember' often means to act on something (Genesis 8:1; Exodus 2:24). When God says he will not remember sins, he means he will not hold them against the people or act against them for them. Hebrews takes this as the decisive line of the prophecy: "Where these have been forgiven, there is no more offering for sin" (10:18). In 10:3 the old sacrifices did the opposite: they called sins to mind every year.

a: he has made the first one old
t: 'Obsolete': does the new covenant replace Israel's?
p: The verse is central to the debate over supersession, the idea that the church replaces Israel.
b: Palaioō means to make or declare old, and it is repeated in 'whatever is made old'. What is aging is 'the first covenant', the Sinai order of priesthood and sacrifice (9:1). Readings differ. (1) Many Christians took it to mean that Judaism itself was finished; Jesper Svartvik's study 'Stumbling Block or Stepping Stone?' (2015) traces how the verse has been used. (2) Calvin read it of the order of Moses 'as far as it was opposed to the dispensation of Christ', so that the ceremonies have ceased. (3) Others read it of the priesthood and offerings, not of God's people, beside Romans 11:29. The Second Vatican Council said 'the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from the Holy Scriptures' (Nostra Aetate 4). Jeremiah's promise itself is made to 'the house of Israel and the house of Judah' (8:8). 'Close to disappearing' may reflect a Temple still standing, or one just destroyed.
orig: πεπαλαίωκεν ... τὸ δὲ παλαιούμενον (pepalaiōken ... to de palaioumenon)

a: a sanctuary that belonged to this world
p: Kosmikon: belonging to the created world, as opposed to the heavenly one; not 'sinful'.
b: The adjective kosmikos describes the earthly tent as part of this world, the realm of things made with hands (9:11, 24). The KJV's 'worldly' can sound like 'sinful' to a modern ear. Hebrews is not calling the tent bad: it was built at God's command and to God's pattern. It belonged to the order that is being shaken (12:27).
orig: τό τε ἅγιον κοσμικόν (to te hagion kosmikon)

a: the loaves that were set out
p: Twelve loaves laid out on the gold table every Sabbath: what Exodus calls the Presence Bread.
b: The Greek says 'the setting out of the loaves' (hē prothesis tōn artōn). Exodus calls them the Presence Bread: "On the table put the Presence Bread, to be in front of me always" (Exodus 25:30). Leviticus 24:5-9 gives twelve loaves, replaced every Sabbath and eaten by the priests. Jesus refers to David eating them (Mark 2:26). The lampstand (Exodus 25:31-40) and the table stood in the outer room with the incense altar (Exodus 40:22-27).

a: This is called the holy place
t: The holy place and the most holy place
p: Hebrews names the two rooms as Exodus does: Hagia, and Hagia Hagiōn, 'holy of holies'.
b: The outer room is Hagia, 'holy place'; the inner room is Hagia Hagiōn, literally 'holy of holies', the Hebrew way of saying 'most holy'. The site's Exodus reads: "The veil will be a dividing line for you between the holy place and the most holy place" (Exodus 26:33). Elsewhere Hebrews uses ta hagia, 'the sanctuary', for the inner room and its heavenly reality (9:8, 12, 24-25), and the Plain English Translation writes 'the sanctuary' there.

a: the second veil
p: The tent had a screen at its door and a veil before the inner room; this is the inner one.
b: Exodus describes a screen at the entrance of the tent (Exodus 26:36) and the veil that hung before the ark (Exodus 26:31-33). The 'second' is the inner veil, the one the high priest passed through on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:2, 12). Hebrews has already called the hope of believers an anchor that goes 'behind the veil' (6:19), and in 10:20 the veil becomes a picture of Christ's flesh. The Gospels tell of the sanctuary curtain torn in two at Jesus' death (Mark 15:38).

a: a golden altar of incense
t: The incense altar inside the most holy place?
p: Exodus puts the incense altar outside the veil; Hebrews seems to put it inside. Five ways readers explain it.
b: Exodus says: "Place the altar in front of the veil that hangs before the ark of the testimony" (Exodus 30:6). Hebrews says the inner tent 'had' (echousa) a golden thymiatērion. (1) The word can mean a censer, and the KJV has 'the golden censer': a fire pan was carried inside on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:12). (2) Calvin took it as the altar of incense, and his English editor added a footnote calling that a mistake and preferring the censer. (3) 'Had' may mean 'belonged to': the altar served the inner room. The site's 1 Kings says Solomon covered "the whole altar that belonged to the inner room" (1 Kings 6:22). (4) The writer is describing from Scripture, not from the Temple, and groups the objects by meaning. (5) Some see a plain error. The Plain English Translation keeps 'altar of incense' and 'had'.

a: In the ark were a golden jar holding the manna, Aaron's staff that had budded, and the tablets of the covenant
p: Exodus and Numbers put the manna and the staff 'in front of' the testimony; Kings says only the tablets were inside.
b: Moses told Aaron to put a jar of manna "in front of the LORD" (Exodus 16:33), and Aaron's staff was put back "in front of the testimony" (Numbers 17:10). By Solomon's day, "Nothing was inside the ark but the two tablets of stone" (1 Kings 8:9). Hebrews follows the tradition that all three were kept in or with the ark. 'Golden' jar is not in the Hebrew of Exodus 16:33; Swete's Septuagint has it (stamnon chrysoun). By the time of the Second Temple the ark was gone: the Mishnah says a stone stood in its place, and the high priest put the incense on it (Mishnah Yoma 5:2).

a: the atonement lid
p: The same Greek word as 'place of atonement' in Romans 3:25; here it is the lid of the ark itself.
b: Hilastērion is the Septuagint's word for the kapporet, the gold lid on the ark where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement. The site calls it 'the atonement lid' (Exodus 25:17-22; Leviticus 16:14). Older English Bibles say 'mercy seat'. Paul uses the same word for Christ: "God put him forward as the place of atonement, through faith, by his blood" (Romans 3:25). Hebrews does not draw the link here, but the whole chapter is about what happened at that lid.

a: Now is not the time to speak about these things one by one
p: A speaker's aside: the furniture matters less than the one entrance into the inner room.
b: This is Claude's reading, not a published one. The sentence sounds like a preacher who could explain every object (the writer has just listed the furniture of both rooms) and chooses not to, because his point lies in the next verses: the inner room was closed to all but one man on one day. The aside supports the view that Hebrews was first spoken aloud, 'a word of exhortation' (13:22). It also warns readers today not to turn the furniture into a code: the writer himself declined to.

a: once a year, and never without blood
p: Only on Yom Kippur did the high priest enter, with the blood of a bull for himself and a goat for the people.
b: Leviticus 16 gives the rite: the high priest offered a bull for his own sins and his household's, brought its blood behind the veil, then did the same with the goat for the people's sin offering (Leviticus 16:11-16). "This is to be a rule for you for all time: atonement is to be made once a year for the Israelites for all their sins" (Leviticus 16:34). The Mishnah tractate Yoma describes how it was done in the Second Temple. Hebrews' argument rests on two details: once a year, and never without blood.

a: the sins the people committed in ignorance
p: Agnoēmata: wrongs done without knowing, or without full intent, which the Law provided atonement for.
b: The Law distinguishes unintentional sins, for which sacrifice was provided (Leviticus 4:2; Numbers 15:27-29), from sins done 'with a high hand', in open defiance (Numbers 15:30-31). Hebrews will draw on the same line in 10:26: for deliberate sin against the truth, 'there is no longer any sacrifice for sins left'. Leviticus 16 says the Day of Atonement covered 'all their sins' (Leviticus 16:16, 21, 34); Hebrews singles out the sins of ignorance.

a: as long as the first tent still stood
p: The outer room, the whole earthly tent, or the whole age it stands for? Each reading has defenders.
b: In 9:2 and 9:6 'the first tent' is the outer room. On that reading, the outer room stood like a barrier in front of the inner one. But the next verse calls it 'a parable for the time now present', and 9:11 contrasts the earthly tent with the 'greater and more perfect tent'. So many read 'first tent' here as the whole earthly sanctuary, and with it the age of the first covenant. 'Still stood' (echousēs stasin) can mean 'still had standing' or validity. Some take the present tenses (the priests 'keep going in', 9:6) as evidence that the Temple was still standing when the writer wrote.
orig: ἔτι τῆς πρώτης σκηνῆς ἐχούσης στάσιν (eti tēs prōtēs skēnēs echousēs stasin)

a: It is a parable for the time now present
p: Parabolē: the tent was a living illustration, pointing beyond itself.
b: The word is the one used for Jesus' parables. The arrangement of the tent, with its closed inner room, was itself a picture. 'The time now present' may mean the writer's own time (the age of the old order still running) or the present time in which the new has come; scholars divide. The same word appears in 11:19, where Abraham got Isaac back 'in a kind of parable'.

a: perfect in his conscience
p: The old sacrifices could cleanse the body for worship, but not the inner self that knows its guilt.
b: 'Make perfect' (teleioō) is a key verb of Hebrews (see 2:10): to bring to the goal, to make fit to stand before God. 'Conscience' (syneidēsis) is the inner knowledge of one's own wrong. The writer's contrast is between flesh and conscience: the ashes and blood made the flesh clean (9:13), but Christ's blood cleans the conscience (9:14; 10:2, 22).

a: different kinds of washing
p: The plural of the word that became 'baptism': here ritual washings of the Law.
b: Baptismos is used for Jewish washings of cups and pots (Mark 7:4) and, in Hebrews 6:2, for 'teaching about washings'. Here it means the Law's washings for purity: of priests (Exodus 29:4), of people after contact with the dead (Numbers 19:17-19), and many more (Leviticus 11-15). 'Rules for the flesh' (dikaiōmata sarkos) does not mean sinful rules; it means rules about the body's purity.

a: until the time came to set things straight
p: Diorthōsis: correction, reform, putting a broken thing right.
b: The word was used for setting a broken bone or reforming laws. The rules were not wrong; they were 'laid on people' for a time, until God set the whole arrangement right. The same thought lies behind Paul's picture of the law as a guardian 'until Christ came' (Galatians 3:24).

a: once for all
p: Not 'once' as in 'one time so far', but once, never to be repeated.
b: Hebrews uses ephapax for Christ's offering (7:27; 9:12; 10:10) and hapax, 'once', in the same sense (9:26, 28). The contrast is with 'every year' (9:25; 10:1, 3) and 'day after day' (10:11). This one word is at the center of the later dispute over the sacrifice of the Mass: see the card at 10:12.

a: eternal redemption
p: Lytrōsis: release by payment, as of a slave or a captive; Christ won a release that never runs out.
b: The word family (lytron, ransom) belongs to the release of slaves and prisoners and to Israel's freeing from Egypt. 'Eternal' (aiōnios) is repeated in this passage: eternal redemption (9:12), the eternal Spirit (9:14), the eternal inheritance (9:15), and at the end, the eternal covenant (13:20). 'Won' renders the middle voice heuramenos, 'having found, obtained for himself'.

a: a heifer's ashes
p: The ashes of a red cow, mixed with water, cleansed people who had touched a dead body.
b: Numbers 19 tells how a red heifer was burned outside the camp with cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet yarn, and its ashes kept "for the water for impurity" (Numbers 19:9). Anyone who had touched a corpse was sprinkled with it. Hebrews puts this rite beside the Day of Atonement because both dealt with uncleanness and both used blood or ashes that were sprinkled. Its point: they made the flesh clean. The same items (scarlet wool, hyssop, sprinkling) return in 9:19.

a: how much more
p: The a fortiori argument, from lesser to greater, that runs through the whole sermon.
b: Jewish teachers called this kind of argument qal vachomer, 'light and heavy': if a thing is true in the lesser case, it is even truer in the greater. Hebrews uses it again and again (2:2-3; 9:13-14; 10:28-29; 12:9, 25). If animal blood made the flesh clean, how much more will Christ's blood clean the conscience. The same form, turned to warning, appears in 10:29.

a: through the eternal Spirit
p: The Holy Spirit, or Christ's own spirit, his inner life that cannot die?
b: The Greek has no article: 'through eternal spirit'. Most readers take it as the Holy Spirit, through whom Jesus did all his work (Luke 4:18; Acts 10:38), and the verse has long been read as a hint of the Trinity: Christ offers himself, to God, through the Spirit. Others read 'his eternal spirit', the inner life by which he offered himself willingly and which death could not hold (7:16, 'the power of a life that cannot be destroyed'). The Plain English Translation capitalizes Spirit with the majority, but both fit the argument: this offering was not of a dumb animal.

a: dead works
p: Deeds that lead to death or have no life in them, from which a conscience needs cleansing.
b: The phrase appeared in 6:1, among the first lessons: 'repentance from dead works'. It probably means sinful deeds that bring death, the opposite of 'good works' (10:24). Some readers take it as the rites of the old order, which cannot give life; the context of cleansing from defilement (a corpse made a person unclean, 9:13) favors sin's deadly works.

a: the eternal inheritance
p: The language of inheritance prepares for the play on 'will' in the next two verses.
b: Klēronomia is what heirs receive. Hebrews calls believers heirs (1:14; 6:17) and Abraham one who would receive a place 'as his inheritance' (11:8). The word leads straight into 9:16-17, where the same Greek word for covenant is used in the sense of a will: an inheritance comes when someone dies.

a: in the case of a will
p: The same Greek word, diathēkē, means both. Here the writer uses its everyday sense: a last will.
b: In everyday Greek diathēkē meant a will, the document that passes on property at death. The Septuagint chose it for the Hebrew berit, 'covenant'. The Plain English Translation says 'covenant' everywhere in Hebrews except here and in 9:17. Readings: (1) The writer plays on the word: a will takes effect at a death, so the new covenant needed Christ's death. Calvin took it this way, saying the Greek word "includes both ideas". (2) It means covenant throughout: covenants were sealed by killing animals (Genesis 15:9-18; Jeremiah 34:18-20), so 'the one who made it' is the sacrificed victim standing for the parties, and 'in the case of the dead' means 'over dead bodies'. The first reading is the most common; the second keeps one meaning through the passage. In 9:17 Westcott and Hort printed mē tote, 'not then', where the other editions have mēpote, 'never': the same letters divided differently.
orig: διαθήκη (diathēkē); ὁ διαθέμενος (ho diathemenos), 'the one who made it'

a: sprinkled both the scroll itself and all the people
t: Blood on the scroll and the people
p: The covenant at Sinai, retold with details from other rites: water, scarlet wool and hyssop.
b: Exodus 24:3-8 tells how Moses read the scroll of the covenant and splashed the blood on the people. Hebrews adds water, scarlet wool, hyssop, and the sprinkling of the scroll and the tent, which Exodus does not mention there. Water, scarlet yarn and hyssop belong to the cleansing rites of Leviticus 14:4-6 and Numbers 19:6, 18. The writer gathers the Law's cleansing rites into one picture. The SBL edition alone leaves out 'and the goats' (see the variant).

a: This is the blood of the covenant
p: Moses' words at Sinai, in a form that sounds like Jesus' words over the cup.
b: Exodus has "Here is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has cut with you" (Exodus 24:8), and Swete's Septuagint begins 'Look' (idou). Hebrews has 'This is' (touto), the same opening as Jesus at the supper: "This is my blood of the covenant" (Mark 14:24). Many think the writer, or the church's worship he knew, shaped Moses' words to echo the Lord's Supper. 'Given you as a command' renders eneteilato, 'commanded', where Exodus says 'cut' or 'made'.

a: no forgiveness comes about without blood being poured out
t: Without the pouring out of blood
p: Haimatekchysia: a word found nowhere before this verse; it may mean shedding blood or pouring it at the altar.
b: The rule echoes Leviticus: "It is the blood that makes atonement, by means of the life in it" (Leviticus 17:11). The rare word haimatekchysia can mean the shedding of blood in death, or the pouring out of blood at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7). The writer says 'almost' everything: the Law also allowed cleansing by water and fire (Numbers 31:23), and a poor person's offering of flour (Leviticus 5:11-13).

a: the heavenly things themselves needed sacrifices better than these
p: The heavenly things are 'made clean' by better sacrifices. Readers ask what in heaven could be unclean.
b: Readings: (1) The heavenly sanctuary is inaugurated or dedicated, as the earthly tent was (9:18-21); 'cleansing' is the language of consecration. (2) Sin defiled the place where God meets his people, as Leviticus 16:16 says of the tent "which stays with them in the middle of their uncleanness" (Leviticus 16:16), so the heavenly meeting place too needs atonement. (3) 'The heavenly things' are the people themselves, God's house (3:6), cleansed in conscience (9:14). (4) The phrase follows the logic of copy and original and should not be pressed. The plural 'sacrifices' generalizes; the writer means Christ's one sacrifice (9:26).

a: a copy of the true one
p: The Greek gives English 'antitype', but here it means the copy, not the fulfillment.
b: Antitypos means something that answers to a typos, a pattern. In later Christian language the 'antitype' is the fulfillment and the 'type' the foreshadowing. Hebrews uses the words the other way around: the heavenly sanctuary is the pattern (8:5), the earthly one is the 'antitype', the copy. 1 Peter 3:21 uses antitypon again, of baptism answering to the flood. Read each in its own sense.

a: to appear now before the face of God on our behalf
p: The high priest went in once a year behind a cloud of incense; Christ appears openly before God for us.
b: On the Day of Atonement the high priest had to cover the atonement lid with a cloud of incense, "so that he does not die" (Leviticus 16:13). Christ appears 'before the face of God' (tō prosōpō tou theou). The thought is the same as 7:25, 'he always lives to intercede for them', and Paul's "He is at God's right hand, and he pleads for us" (Romans 8:34).

a: at the completion of the ages
p: The writer believes he lives at the end of the ages: the last days have begun.
b: Synteleia tōn aiōnōn echoes 1:2, 'in these last days'. The phrase matches Matthew's 'the end of the age' (Matthew 13:39-40; 28:20). For Hebrews the cross stands at the turning point of history; Christ's return (9:28) completes what was begun. 'He has been revealed' (pephanerōtai) refers to his coming in the flesh.
orig: ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ τῶν αἰώνων (epi synteleia tōn aiōnōn)

a: it is in store for human beings to die once, and after this, judgment
p: A verse often used against reincarnation and second chances after death, and in debates on the state of the dead.
b: The writer's point is a comparison: as human beings die once, Christ was offered once (9:28). But the verse has carried more. The Catholic Catechism quotes it against reincarnation: 'we shall not return to other earthly lives', and 'There is no "reincarnation" after death' (paragraph 1013). It also cites it for the 'particular judgment' at death, after which some enter heaven 'through a purification' (paragraph 1022). Others read it as leaving no chance of repentance after death. Some ask whether 'after this' means immediately or at the end of history. The verse does not answer the timing; it sets death and judgment in order. ('It is in store' renders apokeitai, 'is laid up, reserved'.)

a: to bear the sins of many
p: The words come from Isaiah's suffering servant.
b: The site renders the Hebrew of Isaiah 53:12: "He bore the sin of many, / and he will step in for the rebels" (Isaiah 53:12). Hebrews uses anapherō, 'carry up', the verb also used for offering a sacrifice on an altar, so the phrase can mean both 'bear' and 'offer up'. 1 Peter 2:24 uses the same verb: he 'carried up' our sins in his body onto the tree.
orig: εἰς τὸ πολλῶν ἀνενεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας (eis to pollōn anenenkein hamartias)

a: he will be seen a second time, apart from sin
p: As Israel waited for the high priest to come back out of the sanctuary, believers wait for Christ.
b: When a priest went into the sanctuary, the people waited outside for him: "The people kept looking for Zechariah to come out" (Luke 1:21). On the Day of Atonement the high priest's coming back out of the most holy place ended the rite (Leviticus 16:17-18). Hebrews uses that picture for the second coming. 'Apart from sin' means not to deal with sin again, since that was done once; it does not mean he had sin the first time (4:15). This is one of the few places in Hebrews that speaks directly of Christ's return (also 10:25, 37).
orig: ἐκ δευτέρου χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας ὀφθήσεται (ek deuterou chōris hamartias ophthēsetai)

a: not the actual image of the things themselves
p: A shadow is an outline; an image (eikōn) is the real likeness. The law had the first, not the second.
b: The contrast is between skia, a shadow cast ahead of something coming, and eikōn, the true form or likeness of the things themselves. Hebrews has called the Son 'the exact stamp of his being', that is, God's (1:3). The 'good things to come' here are the 'good things that have now come' of 9:11. The law is not called false: a shadow is cast by something real.

a: the offerings would have come to an end, wouldn't they?
p: If the yearly offerings had cleansed for good, they would have stopped. Their repetition shows their limit.
b: The question assumes the offerings are still being made, one of the clues for a date before AD 70. Others answer that the writer describes the system as Scripture presents it, in a timeless present, as the Mishnah, compiled long after the Temple fell, still describes its rites. Either way, the argument is from the repetition itself.

a: There is no way the blood of bulls and goats can take sins away
t: Did the old sacrifices do nothing?
p: Hebrews denies that animal blood takes away sins. What then did the Law's sacrifices do?
b: Leviticus says the priest 'will make atonement' and the sinner 'will be forgiven' (Leviticus 4:20, 26, 31). Readings: (1) The sacrifices worked as God's appointed sign, pointing ahead to Christ, and forgiveness came through what they pointed to (Romans 3:25). (2) They cleansed from ritual impurity, 'the flesh' (9:13), but not the conscience. (3) After the Temple fell, Jewish teachers found another means of atonement in the prophets: Avot de-Rabbi Natan (chapter 4) tells that Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, seeing the Temple in ruins, said 'we have another means of atonement which is as effective, and that is, the practice of lovingkindness', quoting Hosea 6:6 (compare Psalm 51:16-17). The prophets' criticism of empty sacrifice (Psalm 40:6; Isaiah 1:11) is the bridge Hebrews crosses next.

a: but you made a body ready for me
t: 'A body you prepared' or 'ears you dug'?
p: The Hebrew of Psalm 40:6 says 'ears you have dug for me'; the Septuagint in Swete's edition and Hebrews say 'a body'.
b: The site renders the Hebrew: "Sacrifice and grain offering you did not want; / ears you have dug for me" (Psalm 40:6). Opened ears mean a servant who listens and obeys (Isaiah 50:5). Swete's Septuagint (mainly Codex Vaticanus; Psalm 39:7 in the Greek numbering) reads sōma de katērtisō moi, 'but a body you prepared for me', the words Hebrews quotes. How 'ears' became 'body' is debated: a Greek translator's interpretation (the part for the whole: the ear stands for the obedient person), or a change in Greek copying. This note speaks only of Swete's text, not of the other Greek manuscripts of the psalm. Hebrews builds its argument on 'body' (10:10), but the point fits the Hebrew too: God wanted obedience, and the obedience was offered in a body.
orig: σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι (sōma de katērtisō moi); Hebrew אָזְנַיִם כָּרִיתָ לִּי ('oznayim karita li)

a: when he comes into the world, he says
p: Hebrews hears Christ himself speaking David's psalm, at the moment of his coming into the world.
b: The writer often lets God, Christ or the Spirit speak Scripture in the present tense (1:5-13; 2:12-13; 3:7). Here Psalm 40 is the Son's own words to the Father, at his incarnation. Jewish readers take the psalm as David's prayer of thanks; Christian tradition has read its 'I have come' as the Son's coming. Both readings start from the same line: obedience matters more than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22).

a: the scroll of the book has it written about me
p: Kephalis biblou: literally 'a little head' of a book, the Septuagint's way of saying 'the roll of the book'.
b: Kephalis is a diminutive of kephalē, 'head': 'a little head', then an end or a capital, and in the Septuagint 'a roll' (Abbott-Smith's lexicon). In the psalm it may mean the Law of Moses, or a written record of the king's duty (Deuteronomy 17:18). Hebrews takes it as Scripture as a whole, written about the Son. Hebrews drops the psalm's last line, 'your law is in my very core' (Psalm 40:8), and ends at 'to do your will'.

a: He removes the first so that he can set up the second
p: The 'first' is sacrifices; the 'second' is doing God's will. How far does 'removes' reach?
b: Within the quotation, the 'first' is the offerings God did not want, and the 'second' is 'Look, I have come to do your will'. Hebrews reads this as the end of the sacrificial system and its replacement by Christ's obedient offering. The verb anaireō is strong: to take away, abolish. As with 8:13, Christians differ on whether the sentence is about a system of sacrifice or about the whole first covenant, and on what it means for the Jewish people: see the note at 8:13.
orig: ἀναιρεῖ τὸ πρῶτον ἵνα τὸ δεύτερον στήσῃ (anairei to prōton hina to deuteron stēsē)

a: It is by this will that we have been made holy
p: Hagiazō: to set apart for God, to make fit for his presence. The tense says it is done.
b: The perfect tense (hēgiasmenoi esmen) says believers have been made holy and remain so, by the will Christ carried out and the offering of his body. In 10:14 the present participle says they 'are being made holy', and 12:14 tells them to 'go after holiness'. Hebrews holds both: a holiness already given and one still to be pursued. Traditions weigh the two differently (justification and sanctification in Protestant theology; one process of grace in Catholic and Orthodox theology).

a: good for all time
t: For all time: with the sacrifice, or with the sitting?
p: Eis to diēnekes can belong to 'one sacrifice' or to 'took his seat'. The Greek allows both.
b: The phrase sits between the two in Greek. Most English Bibles join it to the sacrifice ('offered for all time a single sacrifice'); some join it to his sitting ('sat down for ever'). The Plain English Translation joins it to the sacrifice. Both say the same thing from two sides: nothing more needs offering, so the priest sits. The same phrase appears in 10:1, of the old sacrifices offered 'for all time', that is, without end, and in 10:14. The Plain English Translation renders it 'for all time' in all three places.

a: set down as a footstool for his feet
t: Until his enemies are set down
p: Psalm 110:1 again: the work of offering is done; the victory is still being worked out.
b: The site's Psalm reads: "until I set your enemies down / as a stool for your feet" (Psalm 110:1). The site's Psalm renders the Hebrew; Hebrews, here and in 1:13, says 'footstool', as Acts 2:35 does with the same Greek words. Paul uses it for the reign of Christ until death itself is defeated (1 Corinthians 15:25-26). The waiting is real: not everything is under him yet (2:8).

a: The Holy Spirit is our witness too
p: Hebrews calls Jeremiah's words the Spirit's testimony, in the present tense, to 'us'.
b: In 8:8 God speaks the prophecy; here the Holy Spirit testifies. In 3:7 the Spirit speaks Psalm 95. For the writer, Scripture is a living voice addressed to the present congregation. The second quotation (10:16-17) is shortened and slightly changed: 'with them' for 'with the house of Israel', and hearts before minds.

a: there is no more offering for sin
p: The end of the argument of chapters 7 to 10. Churches have read it in sharply different ways.
b: Hebrews' conclusion: where Jeremiah's promised forgiveness has come, the offering for sin has done its work. The sentence became central in the Reformation. Calvin, at this verse, wrote that "the Apostle denies that there is now any place for a sacrifice" and attacked the Mass. Catholic teaching agrees that Christ's sacrifice is one and not repeated, and holds that the Mass makes that one sacrifice present rather than adding another. The card at 10:12 sets the churches side by side.

a: So then, brothers
p: Adelphoi addresses the whole congregation, women and men; see the first use at 3:1.
b: The Plain English Translation writes 'brothers', as in Romans and Acts, with the gloss 'brothers and sisters'. The plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of family members or fellow believers. Hebrews also calls Jesus their brother (2:11-12).

a: the boldness to go into the sanctuary
p: Parrēsia was a citizen's right to speak freely; here it is the right to walk into God's presence.
b: In Greek cities parrēsia was the free speech of a citizen in the assembly. Acts uses it for the apostles' courage to speak openly. Hebrews uses it for a believer's right of access: to 'go into the sanctuary', which only the high priest could do once a year (9:7). The word appears at 3:6; 4:16; 10:19, 35, and the Plain English Translation says 'boldness' each time. In 10:35 the readers are told not to throw it away.

a: through the veil, that is, his flesh
p: Is Christ's flesh the veil we pass through, or the way by which we pass?
b: Readings: (1) Christ's flesh is like the veil: his body, torn in death, opened the way, as the Gospels' torn curtain shows (Mark 15:38). (2) 'His flesh' goes with 'the way': the fresh and living way is his body offered (10:10). (3) The veil once hid God; in Christ's human life God is now seen, so the flesh both veils and reveals. 'Fresh' (prosphatos) originally meant newly slaughtered, and 'opened' (enekainisen) is the verb used of dedicating the first covenant (9:18).
orig: διὰ τοῦ καταπετάσματος, τοῦτ' ἔστιν τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ

a: bodies bathed in clean water
p: Most readers hear baptism here; others hear a picture of the priests' washing, applied inwardly.
b: Priests were sprinkled with blood and washed with water before serving (Exodus 29:4, 21; Leviticus 8:6, 30). Hebrews applies this to all believers: hearts sprinkled, bodies washed. Many read 'bodies bathed in clean water' as Christian baptism (compare 1 Peter 3:21; Titus 3:5), and traditions that link baptism with cleansing from sin cite it. Others read the whole verse as a picture of inner cleansing in the language of the priests' consecration. Ezekiel 36:25 promises: clean water, then a new heart.

a: the confession of our hope
p: Homologia: what the church says aloud together about its faith and hope.
b: Hebrews uses homologia three times (3:1; 4:14; 10:23): 'the confession' is a known statement the congregation made. The verb comes back in 13:15, 'lips that confess his name'. Holding it 'never leaning aside' (aklinē) is the opposite of 'drifting away' (2:1).
orig: τὴν ὁμολογίαν τῆς ἐλπίδος ἀκλινῆ (tēn homologian tēs elpidos aklinē)

a: provoke love and good works
p: Paroxysmos usually means a sharp quarrel; here the writer turns it to good.
b: The noun paroxysmos is used of the sharp disagreement between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:39). Here it is a bold choice: provoke one another, but to love. 'Pay attention' (katanoeō) is the verb of 3:1, 'think carefully about Jesus'.

a: We must not walk out on our gatherings
p: Some had stopped meeting. Fear of persecution, shame, or a drift back to the synagogue are the proposals.
b: Episynagōgē, 'gathering together', is related to synagōgē. The writer says some have a habit of staying away. Reasons proposed: fear after persecution (10:32-34), loss of first enthusiasm (5:11-12), the pull of the synagogue or Temple, or division into house groups. 'The Day' is the day of the Lord's coming (10:37; 1 Thessalonians 5:2-4). Many churches cite the verse for regular worship together.

a: if we keep on sinning by choice
p: Who is meant? Hebrews' warnings are read through each church's view of whether a believer can fall away.
b: This is the warning of 6:4-6 again; the card on whether believers can fall away is at that passage. Two readings from the sources: Calvin at this verse says the sin meant is not every sin after conversion but a complete break, those "who willfully renounced fellowship with the Church" and Christ, and he rejects "Novatus and his sect", who used the verse to deny pardon to all "who had fallen after baptism". Wesley's note says the sin is "total apostasy from God", and on 10:29 that the person had been made holy by the covenant's blood, so "Christ died for him also, and he was at least justified once." The 'by choice' echoes the Law's 'high hand' sins (Numbers 15:30-31).
orig: ἑκουσίως γὰρ ἁμαρτανόντων ἡμῶν (hekousiōs gar hamartanontōn hēmōn)

a: the fury of a fire about to eat up those who stand against him
p: The words are close to Isaiah 26:11 as Swete's Septuagint has it.
b: Swete's Septuagint of Isaiah 26:11 reads zēlos lēmpsetai laon apaideuton, kai nyn pyr tous hypenantious edetai, 'zeal will seize an untaught people, and now fire will eat the adversaries'. Hebrews uses 'zeal (fury) of fire' and 'the adversaries'. Fire is God's judgment and God's presence: 'our God really is a devouring fire' (12:29; Deuteronomy 4:24).
orig: πυρὸς ζῆλος ἐσθίειν μέλλοντος τοὺς ὑπεναντίους

a: on the word of two or three witnesses
p: The Law's rule for a death sentence, here for one who led others into idolatry.
b: The rule is in Deuteronomy: "The one who is to die is to be put to death on the word of two witnesses or three witnesses" (Deuteronomy 17:6). The case there is a person who served other gods, so the comparison is exact: abandoning the covenant God. Jesus and Paul use the same rule for church matters (Matthew 18:16; 2 Corinthians 13:1).

a: counted the blood of the covenant, the blood that made him holy, as something common
p: Koinos: common, ordinary, unholy. To treat Christ's blood as ordinary blood.
b: Koinos is the word for 'common' as opposed to 'holy' (Mark 7:2; Acts 10:14). Three charges build: stamping on the Son of God, treating the covenant blood as unholy, insulting the Spirit of grace. 'The blood that made him holy' is a crux in the perseverance debate: was this person a true believer? Arminian and Wesleyan readers say yes; many Reformed readers say he was set apart outwardly by belonging to the covenant people, as Israel was. See 10:26.

a: Vengeance is mine. I will pay back
p: Deuteronomy 32:35 in a form that matches Paul's quotation, not the usual Greek.
b: Paul quotes the same words in the same form: "Vengeance is mine. I will pay back, says the Lord" (Romans 12:19). Both differ from Swete's Septuagint, which reads 'on a day of vengeance I will repay', and stand closer to the Hebrew, "Vengeance belongs to me, and payback" (Deuteronomy 32:35). Paul and Hebrews may share a known form of the verse. The second quotation, "The LORD will judge his people" (Deuteronomy 32:36), means in its setting that God will vindicate his people; here it warns them.

a: you had received the light
p: Phōtizō: 'enlightened', as in 6:4. Later Christians used it for baptism.
b: The same verb describes those 'who once received the light' in 6:4, and the Plain English Translation uses the same words in both places. Here it marks the readers' conversion. Some readers hear baptism in the word; the text itself says only that they had come to the light. 'A great contest' (athlēsis) is a word from the athletic games, preparing for the race of 12:1.

a: put on display like a show in the theater
p: Theatrizomai: to be exposed in the theater, or held up to public shame.
b: The verb comes from theatron, the theater, where public shaming and later executions took place. Paul says the apostles became a spectacle (theatron) to the world (1 Corinthians 4:9). The readers had been publicly mocked; others had stood with them. Proposed occasions: the expulsion of Jews from Rome under Claudius (Acts 18:2 says "Claudius had given orders that all the Jews must leave Rome"), or another local persecution. No one had yet died (12:4).

a: in just a little while, a very little
p: Hebrews opens with words from Isaiah 26:20 and runs straight into Habakkuk 2:3-4.
b: 'A very little while' (mikron hoson hoson) is in Swete's Septuagint of Isaiah 26:20, where God's people hide 'a very little while' until his anger passes. Then Habakkuk: Swete's Greek of Habakkuk 2:3 ends 'coming, he will come and will not delay' (erchomenos hēxei). Hebrews adds the article, 'the one who is coming' (ho erchomenos), so that the vision becomes a person, the coming Christ. The site's Hebrew reads: "It is sure to come; it will not be late" (Habakkuk 2:3).

a: will live by faith
t: My righteous one will live by faith
p: Habakkuk 2:4 in a different form from the Hebrew and from Paul, with its two halves reversed.
b: The site's Hebrew: "But the righteous will live by his faithfulness" (Habakkuk 2:4). The Septuagint, in Swete's edition (mainly Codex Vaticanus), has 'the righteous will live by my faith(fulness)', God's. Hebrews has 'my' with the righteous one: 'my righteous one'. Paul drops 'my' altogether: "The righteous will live by faith" (Romans 1:17). Hebrews also reverses the order of the verse, so that 'if he shrinks back' warns the righteous one himself. The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (KJV) leave out 'my'.
orig: ὁ δὲ δίκαιός μου ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται (ho de dikaios mou ek pisteōs zēsetai)

a: We are people of faith, which keeps the soul safe
p: The verse sets up chapter 11: two kinds of people, those who shrink back and those who have faith.
b: 'Shrinking back' (hypostolē) picks up the verb of 10:38. 'Ruin' (apōleia) is destruction. 'Keeps the soul safe' renders eis peripoiēsin psychēs, 'for the gaining (or preserving) of the soul'. The writer counts his hearers with the faithful: 'we are not'. Chapter 11 then shows what faith looks like.
orig: ὑποστολῆς εἰς ἀπώλειαν ... πίστεως εἰς περιποίησιν ψυχῆς

a: assurance about what is hoped for
p: The word can mean substance, underlying reality, confidence, or a title deed. Each gives faith a different shade.
b: Hypostasis literally means what stands under something. In 1:3 it is God's 'being'; in 3:14 the readers' 'confidence'. Here: (1) 'substance' or 'reality': faith gives present reality to what is hoped for (the KJV's 'substance'); (2) 'assurance' or 'confidence', the inner firmness of the believer; (3) in business papers of the time the word could mean a title deed, proof of ownership. The Plain English Translation says 'assurance' and the gloss offers the others. The verse is a description of what faith does, not a full definition.

a: proof of realities no one can see
p: Elenchos is a legal word: evidence that convicts, a test that proves something true.
b: Elenchos means proof, the evidence that settles a case, or the conviction it produces. With 'what is hoped for' (the future) and 'realities no one can see' (the unseen), the two halves of the verse match the chapter: Noah was warned of things 'no one could see yet' (11:7); Moses held on 'as if he could see the one who cannot be seen' (11:27).
orig: πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων (pragmatōn elenchos ou blepomenōn)

a: were given a good witness
p: Martyreō in the passive: they had witness borne to them, by God and by Scripture.
b: The verb martyreō runs through the chapter (11:2, 4, 5, 39). Its passive means 'to be well spoken of', 'to have a good report', and here the one who speaks is God, through Scripture. Those approved become 'witnesses' themselves in 12:1. The 'people of long ago' (hoi presbyteroi, 'the elders') are Israel's ancestors in faith, not church officers.

a: the ages were set in order by a word from God
p: Does 11:3 teach creation out of nothing? It says the visible world did not come from what appears.
b: 'The ages' (tous aiōnas) can mean the world and its eras, as in 1:2. 'Set in order' (katērtisthai) is the verb of 10:5, 'made ready'. The second clause says the seen world did not come 'out of what appears'. Readings: (1) creation out of nothing (ex nihilo): nothing visible existed before God spoke. The mother in 2 Maccabees says it plainly: "God made them, not from things that were" (2 Maccabees 7:28). (2) Creation from unseen realities: God's word, or an invisible order, stands behind what we see. Either way, the writer says this is known 'by faith', not by observation.
orig: κατηρτίσθαι τοὺς αἰῶνας ῥήματι θεοῦ (katērtisthai tous aiōnas rhēmati theou)

a: a fuller sacrifice than Cain's
p: Genesis does not say why God accepted Abel's gift; Hebrews says it was by faith.
b: Genesis says only: "The LORD looked kindly at Abel and at his gift" (Genesis 4:4). Readings: (1) Abel brought an animal, with blood, and Cain only produce. (2) Abel brought the best, "the firstborn of his flock and of their fat", while Cain brought what was at hand. (3) The difference was in the heart: Abel offered in faith, as Hebrews says, and Cain was already in the wrong (1 John 3:12). 'Fuller' renders pleiona, literally 'more', 'greater'. The KJV and many Bibles say 'more excellent'.

a: And through it he still speaks, though he died.
p: Abel's blood cried from the ground; his faith still speaks through Scripture.
b: The LORD said to Cain: "Your brother's blood has a voice, and it is crying to me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10). Hebrews hears Abel still speaking, and in 12:24 sets Jesus' blood beside his: 'the blood of sprinkling, which speaks better than Abel'.

a: "he was not found, because God had carried him off."
p: Hebrews quotes Genesis 5:24 in the form found in Swete's Septuagint, which says Enoch 'pleased God'; the Hebrew says he 'walked with God'.
b: The site renders the Hebrew: "Enoch walked with God. Then he was gone, for God took him" (Genesis 5:24). Swete's Septuagint reads 'Enoch pleased God, and he was not found, because God moved him', and Hebrews quotes the second half exactly. The Greek's 'pleased God' leads straight into 11:6: without faith it is impossible to please him. 'Carried off' renders metatithēmi, to move from one place to another (the noun is used in 12:27). Jewish tradition made much of Enoch: see the topic and 1 Enoch, which Jude 1:14-15 quotes.

a: that he is, and that he pays back those who search hard for him
p: That God exists, and that he rewards those who seek him.
b: The minimum the writer names is not a long creed: that God 'is' (estin), and that he becomes a 'rewarder' (misthapodotēs, one who pays wages) to those who seek him out. The word family of 'reward' runs through the sermon (2:2; 10:35; 11:26). The verse explains why Enoch's 'pleasing God' (11:5) implies faith.

a: he passed sentence on the world
p: By building the ark in faith, Noah's life became a verdict against the world that did not believe.
b: Katakrinō means to condemn. Noah did not pronounce a sentence; his obedience showed up the unbelief around him, as Jesus says the men of Nineveh will condemn his generation (Matthew 12:41). 'Through it' can refer to the ark or to his faith. 2 Peter 2:5 calls Noah 'a herald of righteousness'. 'Holy fear' renders eulabētheis, reverent caution, the word family of 5:7 and 12:28.

a: he did not know where he was heading
p: God's call to Abram named no destination: 'to the land that I will show you'.
b: The site's Genesis: "Go on your way, out of your land, away from your kin and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you" (Genesis 12:1). Stephen tells the same story (Acts 7:2-4). 'Did as he was told' renders hypēkousen, 'obeyed': faith in Hebrews is never only belief; it is trust that acts. 'When God called him' renders a passive, 'being called' (kaloumenos); God is the caller understood, as in Genesis 12:1.

a: he settled as a resident alien in the promised land
t: Resident alien in his own land
p: Paroikeō: to live as a foreigner with no citizen's rights. Abraham owned only a grave in Canaan.
b: The verb comes from paroikos, 'resident alien', the legal status of a foreigner allowed to live in a place without citizenship. Abraham told the Hittites: "I am a foreigner living among you as a settler" (Genesis 23:4). 'In tents' uses skēnai, the same word as the tabernacle: the patriarchs lived in tents, as God did among Israel. 1 Peter calls believers "resident aliens and temporary residents" (1 Peter 2:11).

a: the city with foundations, the city whose architect and maker is God
p: Tents have no foundations; Abraham waited for a city God himself would build.
b: The contrast is between the patriarchs' movable tents and a permanent city. Genesis does not say Abraham hoped for a heavenly city; Hebrews reads his whole life as pointing to one (11:16; 12:22; 13:14). Technitēs (craftsman, designer) and dēmiourgos (maker, builder) were words Greek writers used for the maker of the world. The city appears again as 'heavenly Jerusalem' (12:22) and 'the one that is coming' (13:14), and in Revelation 21.

a: a man whose body was already as good as dead
p: Paul uses the same word for Abraham's body: nenekrōmenon, 'already dead'.
b: Paul uses the same verb: Abraham "looked at his own body, which was dead" (Romans 4:19). The stars and the sand come from God's promise in Genesis 22:17, and Hebrews' second half follows that verse in Swete's Septuagint closely (hōs tēn ammon tēn para to cheilos tēs thalassēs, 'as the sand by the lip of the sea').

a: foreigners and temporary residents on the earth
p: Xenoi kai parepidēmoi: people away from home, staying for a while. 1 Peter uses the second word for believers.
b: Xenos is a stranger or foreigner; parepidēmos is someone staying temporarily in a place not his own. Abraham called himself a foreigner and settler (Genesis 23:4); David prayed, "For I am a foreigner with you, / a lodger, as all my fathers were" (Psalm 39:12). 1 Peter writes to "the chosen temporary residents of the Dispersion" (1 Peter 1:1). Readers debate whether these words in 1 Peter describe the readers' real social status or a spiritual picture; in Hebrews 11 the picture is plainly of life on earth before the promised homeland.
r: Genesis 23:4; 1 Chronicles 29:15; Psalm 39:12; 1 Peter 1:1; 1 Peter 2:11; Philippians 3:20

a: God is not ashamed of them, not ashamed to be named as their God
t: The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
p: God names himself by these wanderers: 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob'.
b: At the bush God said he was the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Exodus 3:6, 15). Jesus used the same name to argue for the resurrection: God is not the God of the dead but of the living (Mark 12:26-27). Hebrews says God was not ashamed to be named this way, because he has prepared a city for them. In 2:11 the Son 'is not ashamed' to call believers brothers.

a: his only son
p: Monogenēs: Isaac was not Abraham's only son, but the unique son of the promise.
b: Abraham also had Ishmael, and later sons by Keturah. Genesis has God say "your only one" (Genesis 22:2), and Hebrews uses monogenēs, the word John uses of Jesus (John 1:14, 18; 3:16). The Plain English Translation says 'only son' here, as it does in John 3:16. The word can mean 'only' in number or 'one of a kind', and here it cannot mean that Abraham had no other son. Isaac was the only son through whom the promise ran (11:18).

a: "It is through Isaac that offspring will be named for you."
p: The quotation is Genesis 21:12, word for word as the site's Genesis and the Greek have it.
b: God said to Abraham about Hagar and Ishmael: "for it is through Isaac that offspring will be named for you" (Genesis 21:12). Paul quotes the same line (Romans 9:7). The test of Genesis 22 set God's command against God's promise. Hebrews says Abraham solved it by trusting that God could keep both.

a: in a kind of parable, he did get him back
t: Isaac received back as a parable
p: Abraham received Isaac 'as from the dead', and the scene became a picture of resurrection.
b: 'In a kind of parable' renders en parabolē, the word used in 9:9 for the tent. Readings: (1) 'figuratively speaking': Isaac did not die, but it was as if Abraham got him back from death. (2) The event was a parable, a foreshadowing of Christ's death and resurrection, as many Christian readers have taken the binding of Isaac. Genesis 22:5 has Abraham say, "We will worship, and then we will come back to you" (Genesis 22:5), plural, which Hebrews' reading fits. Jewish tradition reflects on the Akedah (the 'binding') in prayer and liturgy as Israel's great example of faithful obedience.

a: he bowed down over the top of his staff
p: The Hebrew of Genesis 47:31 says 'bed'; the Greek read the same letters as 'staff'. Hebrews follows the Greek.
b: The site renders the Hebrew: "And Israel bowed down at the head of the bed" (Genesis 47:31). The Hebrew letters mṭh can be read mittah, 'bed' (the Masoretic vowels) or matteh, 'staff'. Swete's Septuagint reads 'Israel bowed down on the top of his staff' (epi to akron tēs rhabdou autou), and Hebrews quotes those words. The scene in Hebrews is also a different one: Hebrews joins the bowing to Jacob's blessing of Joseph's sons (Genesis 48). 'Bowed down' (prosekynēsen) also means 'worshiped'.
orig: προσεκύνησεν ἐπὶ τὸ ἄκρον τῆς ῥάβδου αὐτοῦ (prosekynēsen epi to akron tēs rhabdou autou)

a: spoke of the going out of the sons of Israel
p: Joseph believed God would bring Israel out of Egypt and asked to be carried along. The Greek word is exodos.
b: "God will surely come to help you. When he does, carry my bones up from here" (Genesis 50:25). Moses took the bones at the exodus (Exodus 13:19), and they were buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32). 'Going out' is exodos, the word that gave the book of Exodus its name, and the word Luke uses for Jesus' 'departure' in Luke 9:31.

a: They saw he was a fine child
p: Asteios: 'fine, well-formed'. The same word is in Swete's Septuagint of Exodus 2:2.
b: The site's Exodus reads: "She saw him, that he was good, and she hid him three months" (Exodus 2:2). Swete's Septuagint has 'seeing that he was fine' (asteion), the word Hebrews uses, and puts the hiding in the plural, 'they hid him', which Hebrews also follows ('his parents'). Stephen uses the same word: Moses was 'fine in God's sight' (Acts 7:20).

a: the disgrace of the Messiah
t: Moses and 'the disgrace of the Messiah'
p: How could Moses bear the disgrace of Christ centuries before Jesus?
b: The phrase may echo Psalm 89:50-51 as Swete's Septuagint has it (88:51-52 in the Greek), where the disgrace of God's servants and the insults thrown at 'your anointed' (tou christou sou) stand together. The site's Hebrew reads: "the insults they have thrown at the footprints of your anointed" (Psalm 89:51). Readings: (1) 'the Messiah' here means God's anointed people, Israel, whose shame Moses shared. (2) Moses suffered the same kind of disgrace Christ later bore, for God's sake. (3) Moses had some foresight of the coming Christ (John 5:46 has Jesus say Moses wrote about him). (4) Christ was present with Israel in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:4). 13:13 calls believers to bear 'his disgrace' too.
orig: τὸν ὀνειδισμὸν τοῦ Χριστοῦ (ton oneidismon tou Christou)

a: unafraid of the king's rage
t: Did Moses leave Egypt in fear?
p: Exodus 2:14-15 says Moses was afraid and fled; Hebrews says he was not afraid. Which leaving is meant?
b: After killing the Egyptian, "Moses was afraid" and fled from Pharaoh (Exodus 2:14-15). Readings: (1) Hebrews means the exodus itself, when Moses defied Pharaoh and led Israel out openly (Exodus 10:28-29; Exodus 12:31); against this, the Passover (11:28) came before the exodus, though the writer may not keep strict order. (2) Hebrews means the flight to Midian: Moses feared for his life, but the king's anger did not turn him back from choosing God's people (11:25). (3) Hebrews reads Moses' whole life as one act of faith and does not point to a single moment. 'Kept going strong' renders ekarterēsen, 'endured, held firm'.
orig: μὴ φοβηθεὶς τὸν θυμὸν τοῦ βασιλέως (mē phobētheis ton thymon tou basileōs)

a: the splashing of the blood
p: The blood on the doorposts kept 'the destroyer' away from Israel's firstborn.
b: "I will see the blood and pass over you, and no blow will fall on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt" (Exodus 12:13). Exodus 12:23 calls the agent "the destroyer". 'Splashing' renders proschysis, a pouring or smearing on. The perfect tense 'he kept' (pepoiēken) may hint that the Passover is still kept.
orig: τὴν πρόσχυσιν τοῦ αἵματος (tēn proschysin tou haimatos)

a: the Red Sea
t: Red Sea or Sea of Reeds
p: The Greek says 'Red Sea' (Erythra Thalassa), as the Septuagint does; the Hebrew says Yam Suf.
b: The Hebrew of Exodus calls the sea Yam Suf, usually rendered 'Sea of Reeds'. The Septuagint translated it 'Red Sea', and the New Testament follows the Greek (also Acts 7:36). On the location, see the topic. The Israelites "went into the middle of the sea on dry ground" (Exodus 14:22).

a: Rahab the prostitute
t: Rahab: faith in Hebrews, works in James
p: Hebrews praises Rahab's faith; James asks whether she was 'justified by works'. Both name the same deed.
b: Rahab hid the spies (Joshua 2) and confessed that "the LORD your God, he is God in the sky above and on the earth below" (Joshua 2:11). Hebrews names her faith; James says: "Rahab the prostitute was the same. She took in the messengers and sent them away by a different road. Was she not justified by works?" (James 2:25). Both point to the welcome she gave. The Greek pornē, here, in James and in Swete's Septuagint of Joshua 2:1, means prostitute. Matthew lists a Rahab in Jesus' family line (Matthew 1:5).

a: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel
p: The list includes Samson and Jephthah, whose stories are troubling. Why are they here?
b: The order does not follow the book of Judges (Barak comes before Gideon there, and Jephthah before Samson). Each had a moment of trust: Gideon with three hundred men (Judges 7), Barak who would not go without Deborah but went (Judges 4), Samson's last prayer (Judges 16:28-30), Jephthah, who trusted God against the Ammonites but made a terrible vow (Judges 11). Hebrews does not praise everything they did; it says God worked through their faith. Some readers find comfort here; others think the writer's list is a quick roll call and should not be pressed.

a: shut lions' mouths
p: Daniel in the lions' den, the three friends in the furnace, prophets who escaped the sword.
b: "My God sent his angel to shut the lions' mouths" (Daniel 6:22); Samson and David also killed lions (Judges 14:6; 1 Samuel 17:34-37). 'Put out the power of fire' (11:34) recalls the furnace: "The fire had had no power over their bodies" (Daniel 3:27). 'Mouths of the sword' is a Hebrew way of saying the sword's edge, and the Plain English Translation keeps 'mouths' to show the echo with the lions. Elijah and Elisha escaped the sword (1 Kings 19:1-3; 2 Kings 6:31-32).
r: Daniel 6:22; Daniel 3:19-27; Judges 14:6; 1 Samuel 17:34-37; 1 Kings 19:1-3; 2 Kings 6:31-32

a: Women got their dead back by resurrection
t: Sons given back to their mothers
p: Elijah and Elisha raised widows' sons; the Maccabean mother hoped to receive her sons back.
b: "See," said Elijah, "your son is living" (1 Kings 17:23). Elisha said to the woman from Shunem, "Lift up your son" (2 Kings 4:36). These came back to this life. The 'better resurrection' in the next sentence is the resurrection to life forever, which the martyrs of 2 Maccabees hoped for.

a: Others were tortured on the rack
p: The verb comes from tympanon, the frame on which Eleazar died in 2 Maccabees 6.
b: In 2 Maccabees, the old scribe Eleazar refused to eat pork and "went at once to the torture frame" (2 Maccabees 6:28); the Greek word is tympanon, the root of Hebrews' verb etympanisthēsan. The king offered the youngest of seven brothers riches and favor if he would leave his ancestral ways (2 Maccabees 7:24): 'would not take the release'. The brothers died hoping for resurrection: "the King of the world will raise us, who died for his laws, to live again forever" (2 Maccabees 7:9). 2 Maccabees is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians and part of the Apocrypha for Protestants.

a: They were sawed in two
p: Jewish tradition told that King Manasseh had Isaiah sawn in two; Hebrews may allude to it.
b: The Old Testament does not tell of any prophet sawn in two. The Babylonian Talmud tells that Isaiah, fleeing Manasseh, was swallowed by a cedar tree, and Manasseh's servants "brought the cedar tree and sawed through it" (Yevamot 49b). The Martyrdom of Isaiah, a Jewish story kept in the Christian Ascension of Isaiah, says they "sawed in sunder Isaiah, the son of Amoz, with a wood-saw" (in R. H. Charles's 1913 translation). Neither is Scripture for any church. The verb names no one, so Hebrews may allude to this story. 'Stoned' recalls Zechariah son of Jehoiada (2 Chronicles 24:21); 'by murder with the sword' recalls the prophets Elijah mourned (1 Kings 19:10) and Uriah (Jeremiah 26:23).
r: 2 Chronicles 24:20-22; 1 Kings 19:10; Jeremiah 26:23; Matthew 23:35-37; Ascension of Isaiah 5

a: sheepskins and goat hides
p: Elijah's cloak in the Greek is a mēlōtē, a sheepskin, the word Hebrews uses here.
b: In Swete's Septuagint, Elijah wraps his face "in his sheepskin" (en tē mēlōtē, 1 Kings 19:13), and Elisha takes up the same cloak (2 Kings 2:13-14). Hebrews' mēlōtai points to prophets like Elijah, homeless and hunted. The site's Hebrew calls it his "cloak" (1 Kings 19:13).

a: The world was not worth them
p: The verse reverses the world's verdict: the outcasts were worth more than the world that cast them out.
b: This is Claude's reflection, not a published argument. Hebrews uses the language of honor and shame throughout (10:33; 11:26; 12:2; 13:13). The world judged these people worthless and drove them to deserts and caves; Hebrews says the world was not worthy of them. For a congregation that had been shamed in public (10:33), the sentence offered a new way to count honor, the same move as Jesus scorning the shame of the cross (12:2).

a: did not receive the promise
t: They did not receive the promise
p: But in 6:15 Abraham 'came to get what was promised'. How do the two fit?
b: In 6:15 Abraham, 'by being patient, came to get what was promised', meaning Isaac and the oath. Here none of the heroes received 'the promise', meaning its final fulfillment: the city, the homeland, the perfection that comes through Christ. Readers distinguish promises (plural, 11:13, 33) kept in history from 'the promise' (singular) kept at the end.

a: so that they would not be made perfect without us
p: The heroes of faith wait for the church; both are made perfect together. When?
b: 'Made perfect' is Hebrews' verb for reaching God's goal (2:10; 10:14). The heroes are not left behind, but they reach the goal with 'us'. When? (1) At the final resurrection, when all are raised together. (2) Already now, through Christ's offering: 12:23 speaks of 'the spirits of righteous people who have been made perfect' in the heavenly city. Many readers combine the two. The verse also says something about Israel and the church: the faithful of Israel and the believers in Jesus form one company.
orig: ἵνα μὴ χωρὶς ἡμῶν τελειωθῶσιν (hina mē chōris hēmōn teleiōthōsin)

a: a cloud of witnesses
p: Spectators in a stadium, or people who give testimony? The word allows both.
b: Martys means one who gives testimony; in this chapter the people of chapter 11 'were given a good witness' (11:2, 39). The setting is a race, so many readers picture a stadium crowd watching. Others stress that the witnesses do not so much watch us as testify to us, by their lives, that faith endures. 'Cloud' was a common picture for a great crowd. Later the word martys came to mean 'martyr'.

a: the sin that wraps itself around us so easily
p: Euperistatos: a rare word, 'readily besetting'; the Plain English Translation pictures sin wrapping around a runner.
b: The word is found nowhere else in the New Testament. Abbott-Smith's lexicon gives 'readily besetting' (the KJV has 'the sin which doth so easily beset us'). The picture of a runner stripping off clothing and weights fits a sin that wraps around and trips. 'Every burden' (onkon) is any weight, not only sin.

a: the Founder and perfecter of faith
p: Archēgos: the founder, leader, pioneer who goes first; teleiōtēs: the one who brings it to completion.
b: The site renders archēgos 'Founder', as in Acts 3:15 (the Founder of life) and Hebrews 2:10. The word means a leader who opens the way for others: a pioneer, a champion, the founder of a city or family. Teleiōtēs, 'perfecter, completer', belongs with the book's verb 'make perfect'. 'Faith' has the article, 'the faith': Jesus is both the one who began and finished the race of faith himself, and the one who brings others' faith to its goal. The Plain English Translation does not add 'our'.
orig: τὸν τῆς πίστεως ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν Ἰησοῦν

a: For the joy that lay ahead of him
t: For the joy, or instead of the joy?
p: The Greek preposition anti can mean 'for the sake of' or 'in place of'. Both readings have defenders.
b: Reading 1: Jesus endured the cross for the sake of the joy set before him, the joy of the throne and of bringing many sons to glory (2:10). Reading 2: Jesus endured the cross instead of the joy he could have had, choosing suffering over present happiness, as Moses chose ill treatment over sin's pleasures (11:25-26). In 12:16 the same word anti means 'in exchange for' (Esau sold his birthright 'for' one meal). The Plain English Translation's 'for the joy' keeps both readings open, as the Greek does.
orig: ἀντὶ τῆς προκειμένης αὐτῷ χαρᾶς (anti tēs prokeimenēs autō charas)

a: scorning its shame
p: Crucifixion was meant to shame. Jesus 'scorned' the shame: he counted it as nothing.
b: Crucifixion was a public death meant to disgrace. Deuteronomy 21:23 adds a curse on one hanged on a tree (Galatians 3:13). 'Scorning' (kataphronēsas) means despising, treating as of no weight. The readers had faced public shame (10:33); Jesus shows them how to treat it.

a: to the point of blood
t: Not yet to the point of blood
p: None of the readers had yet been killed for their faith.
b: The phrase can mean resisting to the point of being wounded, or of dying. It fits 10:32-34: insults, prison, loss of property, but no deaths. That is one reason many date the letter before the deaths of Christians in Rome under Nero (AD 64), or set it in a church that had escaped them. The fight here is 'against sin', which may mean the pressure to deny the faith.

a: My son, do not think little of the Lord's discipline
p: The quotation follows Swete's Septuagint of Proverbs, which differs from the Hebrew in its last line.
b: The site renders the Hebrew: "The LORD's discipline, my son, do not reject, / and do not recoil from his rebuke" (Proverbs 3:11). In 3:12 the Hebrew reads "the way a father treats the son he takes pleasure in" (Proverbs 3:12); Swete's Septuagint has 'he whips every son he takes in'. Hebrews follows Swete's Septuagint here (which has 'rebukes' where Hebrews has 'disciplines'). The writer calls Proverbs an 'exhortation' that speaks to the readers as sons, in the present tense.

a: What you are enduring is for your discipline
p: Hebrews calls the readers' hardships God's training. Readers differ on how far to apply it.
b: Paideia means the whole upbringing of a child: teaching, training and correction. The readers' troubles were persecution for their faith (10:32-34), not punishment for a particular sin. Readings: (1) God sends or allows hardship to train his children; (2) God uses hardship that comes from others, without causing it. Some caution against using these verses to tell sufferers that their pain is deserved; the passage itself presents discipline as a sign of being loved and accepted as sons.

a: not sons at all
p: Nothoi: children born outside a lawful marriage, who had no right to inherit.
b: In Greek and Roman law, a nothos (illegitimate son) had no share in the family inheritance and a father had no duty to raise him. The point is pastoral: discipline proves that a father counts you as his heir. 'Partners' (metochoi) is the word of 3:1, 14 and 6:4.

a: the Father of spirits
p: A title for God as the source of every life, set against human 'fathers of our flesh'.
b: Moses and Aaron prayed, "God, God of the spirits of all flesh" (Numbers 16:22). Hebrews contrasts the fathers of our flesh with the Father of spirits. The writer's point is that obeying such a Father leads to life.
orig: τῷ πατρὶ τῶν πνευμάτων (tō patri tōn pneumatōn)

a: a peaceful fruit, righteousness
p: Gegymnasmenois: exercised, trained, as in the gymnasium.
b: Hebrews used the same verb for mature people whose senses are 'trained' (5:14). The picture of athletic training ties chapter 12 together: the race (12:1), the contest (12:4), the training (12:11), the weak knees and level track (12:12-13). 'The peaceful fruit of righteousness' may mean that righteousness is the fruit, as the Plain English Translation takes it, or that the fruit is peace that comes with righteousness.

a: straighten up the hands that hang slack
p: Words from Isaiah 35:3, where exiles are told that God is coming to save them.
b: The site's Isaiah: "Put strength into slack hands, / and steady knees that wobble" (Isaiah 35:3). The Septuagint of Isaiah (Swete's edition, mainly Codex Vaticanus) has cheires aneimenai kai gonata paralelymena. Hebrews has the same 'hands' and 'knees' and the same second word (paralelymena); its first word, pareimenas, is a close synonym of Isaiah's. In Isaiah the next lines say "Here is your God" coming to save. 12:13 then draws on Proverbs 4:26, which the site renders "Level the track your foot walks on" (Proverbs 4:26).

a: without it no one will see the Lord
t: Holiness without which no one will see the Lord
p: A sentence that churches read through their teaching on holiness and grace.
b: 'Holiness' here is hagiasmos, the process or state of being made holy (the same family as 10:10, 14). Some read it as a call to a life made wholly holy in this life; others as the holiness that always comes with saving faith, not a condition earned; others as lifelong growth in holiness by grace. Jesus' beatitude stands behind it: the pure in heart will see God (Matthew 5:8).
orig: τὸν ἁγιασμόν, οὗ χωρὶς οὐδεὶς ὄψεται τὸν κύριον

a: no root of bitterness shoots up and makes trouble
p: Deuteronomy 29:18 in the Greek, with a play on two similar words.
b: The site's Hebrew: "Take care that no root is here among you that bears poison and wormwood" (Deuteronomy 29:18). Swete's Septuagint has rhiza anō phyousa en cholē kai pikria, 'a root growing up in gall and bitterness'. Hebrews has rhiza pikrias anō phyousa enochlē, 'makes trouble': enochlē and en cholē look almost alike. In Deuteronomy the root is a person who turns to other gods and leads others with him: a warning against apostasy.
orig: ῥίζα πικρίας ἄνω φύουσα ἐνοχλῇ (rhiza pikrias anō phyousa enochlē)

a: sexually immoral, or treats holy things as nothing, as Esau did
p: Genesis does not say so. Is 'as Esau did' attached to both words, or only to the second?
b: Genesis tells of Esau's foreign wives (Genesis 26:34-35), not of sexual sin. Readings: (1) 'as Esau' goes only with bebēlos, 'profane, treating holy things as common'. (2) Both words describe Esau, following Jewish tradition that blackened him. The Babylonian Talmud says that on the day he sold his birthright Esau "committed five transgressions", the first being that he "engaged in sexual intercourse with a betrothed maiden" (Bava Batra 16b). (3) 'Sexually immoral' is used in the Old Testament picture of unfaithfulness to God. The Plain English Translation keeps the order of the Greek.
orig: πόρνος ἢ βέβηλος ὡς Ἠσαῦ (pornos ē bebēlos hōs Ēsau)

a: he sold his own birthright
p: Esau traded his rights as firstborn for a bowl of stew.
b: "So he swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob" (Genesis 25:33). Genesis closes: "So Esau despised the birthright" (Genesis 25:34). The firstborn received a double share and the father's chief blessing. Hebrews calls believers 'the assembly of the firstborn' (12:23): the readers are in danger of trading their own birthright for relief from present hunger.

a: He found no place for repentance
p: Esau wept for the blessing. Was it his own change of heart he could not find, or a change of Isaac's mind?
b: Genesis: "Esau raised his voice and wept" (Genesis 27:38), but Isaac had said of Jacob, "blessed he will be" (Genesis 27:33). Readings: (1) Esau could not undo his choice; Isaac would not reverse the blessing, so there was 'no place' to change the outcome. (2) Esau sought repentance itself and could not find it, because his sorrow was for the loss, not for despising what was holy. 'It' (autēn) can refer to 'repentance' or to 'the blessing'; both are feminine. The verse belongs with the warnings of 6:4-6 and 10:26-31.
orig: μετανοίας γὰρ τόπον οὐχ εὗρεν (metanoias gar topon ouch heuren)

a: a fire burning, black darkness, deep gloom and a whirlwind
p: The fire, darkness, trumpet and voice come from Exodus 19-20 and Deuteronomy 4-5.
b: Moses reminded Israel: "The mountain was burning with fire up into the heart of the sky, with darkness, cloud and deep gloom" (Deuteronomy 4:11). At Sinai there was "the blast of a ram's horn, extremely loud" (Exodus 19:16), and the people begged: "Let God not speak with us, for fear we die" (Exodus 20:19). Hebrews does not name Sinai.
