Its point is that Sinai could be touched, a physical mountain, and was terrifying. Some manuscripts add 'mountain' after 'touch' (see the Byzantine text and the KJV).

a: They could not stand what was being commanded
p: A short form of Exodus 19:12-13. The Byzantine text adds 'or shot through with an arrow'.
b: Exodus: "He must be stoned or shot, animal or human; he must not live" (Exodus 19:13). Hebrews gives only the part about the animal. The Textus Receptus adds 'or thrust through with a dart' found in Swete's Septuagint of Exodus 19:13 (ē bolidi katatoxeuthēsetai), which the KJV prints. The holiness that made the mountain deadly to touch is the holiness the readers now approach, not by touching but by grace.

a: "I am full of terror, and I am shaking."
p: The first words are from Deuteronomy 9:19, where Moses feared God's anger after the golden calf.
b: Exodus does not record Moses saying he was afraid at Sinai. The words 'I am full of terror' (ekphobos eimi) are found in Swete's Septuagint of Deuteronomy 9:19, where Moses remembers the golden calf: the site renders the Hebrew "For I was afraid of the anger and the rage the LORD had against you" (Deuteronomy 9:19). Hebrews joins that fear to the scene at the mountain. The Septuagint of Deuteronomy 9:19 (Swete's edition, mainly Codex Vaticanus) has only 'I am full of terror'; 'and I am shaking' (kai entromos) is not there.
orig: Ἔκφοβός εἰμι καὶ ἔντρομος (ekphobos eimi kai entromos)

a: Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, heavenly Jerusalem
p: Not the hill in Jerusalem but the city it stood for: God's dwelling, and the readers' true home.
b: Zion was the hill of David's city and the Temple, and the prophets used it for the place where God reigns (Psalm 2:6; Isaiah 2:2-3; Micah 4:1-2). Paul speaks of "The Jerusalem above" (Galatians 4:26), and Revelation sees "the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven" (Revelation 21:2). Note the tense: 'you have come near'. The readers already stand, in worship, at the city Abraham waited for (11:10, 16).
r: Psalm 2:6; Isaiah 2:2-3; Micah 4:1-2; Galatians 4:26; Revelation 14:1; Revelation 21:2; 11:10, 16; 13:14

a: to a festive gathering
p: Panēgyris: a festival crowd. The punctuation decides whether it describes the angels or the assembly.
b: Panēgyris was a festival assembly, such as the crowds at the Olympic games or a city feast. Greek manuscripts had little punctuation, so editors decide: (1) 'tens of thousands of angels in festive gathering', the angels celebrating; (2) 'to a festive gathering and assembly of the firstborn', the joyful assembly of believers; (3) each item in the list stands alone, as the Plain English Translation sets it. The KJV's 'general assembly' renders the same word. The contrast with Sinai is the point: fear and darkness there, festival here.

a: the assembly of the firstborn whose names are listed in the heavens
p: Angels, the faithful of Israel, or all believers? The words fit the church, God's firstborn people.
b: Ekklēsia is the word for 'church'; here it is the heavenly assembly. 'Firstborn' (plural) recalls Israel, God's firstborn ("Israel is my son, my firstborn", Exodus 4:22), and the birthright Esau threw away (12:16). Readings: (1) angels, already named before; (2) the saints of the old covenant; (3) all believers, living and dead, whose names are 'listed in the heavens', as Jesus told his disciples to rejoice that "your names stand written in heaven" (Luke 10:20). Most readers take the third.

a: the spirits of righteous people who have been made perfect
p: A verse about the dead, already 'made perfect' and present in the heavenly city.
b: The faithful who have died are called 'spirits' and are 'made perfect', the goal 11:40 said they would reach together with us. Readers cite the verse in several debates. (1) The intermediate state: the dead in Christ are conscious and with God before the resurrection of the body. (2) Those who hold that the soul sleeps or rests until the resurrection read 'made perfect' as a statement of their secure standing, not of present experience. (3) The communion of saints: worship on earth joins the worship of heaven, where the faithful departed already are. The verse does not describe where or how the dead are, only that the worshiping church has 'come near' to them.

a: the blood of sprinkling, which speaks better than Abel
t: Blood that speaks better than Abel
p: Abel's blood cried for justice; Jesus' blood speaks of forgiveness and access.
b: "Your brother's blood has a voice, and it is crying to me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10). Hebrews says Jesus' blood 'speaks better than Abel', that is, than Abel's blood, or than Abel himself, who 'still speaks' (11:4). 'The blood of sprinkling' recalls the covenant at Sinai (9:19-21) and the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14). The new covenant here uses neos, 'new, recent', where 8:8 and 9:15 have kainos, 'new in kind'.
orig: αἵματι ῥαντισμοῦ κρεῖττον λαλοῦντι παρὰ τὸν Ἅβελ

a: the one who speaks from the heavens
t: Do not refuse the one speaking
p: God spoke at Sinai on earth; now he speaks from heaven. The argument is 'how much more' again.
b: 'Turn down' (paraiteomai) is the verb of 12:19, where the people at Sinai 'begged' that no more words be spoken: the same verb, used first for pleading and then for refusing. The writer's 'how much more' (2:2-3; 10:28-29) turns to its final form: if refusing the voice on earth was deadly, refusing the voice from heaven is worse.

a: "Once more I will shake not only the earth but heaven too."
p: Haggai promised a shaking of heaven and earth before the glory of God's house. Hebrews reads the words 'once more'.
b: The site's Haggai: "Once more, in a little while, I am about to shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry ground" (Haggai 2:6). The Septuagint (Swete's edition, mainly Codex Vaticanus) has Eti hapax egō seisō, 'yet once I will shake', the words Hebrews quotes, and Hebrews rearranges the rest to 'not only the earth but also heaven' to stress what is new. In Haggai the shaking brings the nations' treasures to the rebuilt Temple. Hebrews hears in 'once more' a final, one-time shaking of the created order.
r: Haggai 2:6-7; Haggai 2:21-22; Exodus 19:18; Judges 5:4-5; Psalm 68:8; Isaiah 13:13

a: the things that are shaken will be moved away
p: Will the created world be destroyed, or transformed? The verse is cited on both sides.
b: 'Moved away' renders metathesis, the noun used for Enoch being 'carried off' (11:5) and for the 'change' of law in 7:12: a transfer or removal, not necessarily destruction. Readings: (1) The present creation will pass away and be replaced (2 Peter 3:10; Revelation 21:1). (2) What is shaken loose is everything temporary and sinful, while creation itself is renewed (Romans 8:21). (3) The 'shaken things' are the old covenant's earthly order (Sinai, the tent), and the unshaken kingdom is the new covenant. 'Things that were made' sets the shakable against God's own kingdom.
orig: τῶν σαλευομένων μετάθεσιν ὡς πεποιημένων (tōn saleuomenōn metathesin hōs pepoiēmenōn)

a: let us give thanks
t: Give thanks, or hold on to grace?
p: Echōmen charin: 'let us have thanks' (be grateful), or 'let us hold on to grace'.
b: The phrase echein charin is the normal Greek idiom for being grateful (Luke 17:9; 1 Timothy 1:12). The KJV renders it literally: 'let us have grace'. Both fit: grace given is the reason for thanks, and 'through it' (di' hēs) comes the worship that pleases God.

a: For our God really is a devouring fire
p: Deuteronomy 4:24, quoted to close the warning.
b: "For the LORD your God is a devouring fire, a jealous God" (Deuteronomy 4:24). In Deuteronomy the words warn against idols; here they warn against turning away. The same God who calls them to Zion is the God of Sinai's fire. Hebrews does not set a gentle God of the new covenant against a harsh God of the old.

a: Let love for the brothers remain
p: Philadelphia: the love of brothers and sisters, used in the New Testament for love between believers.
b: In Greek, philadelphia was love between siblings. Christians used it for the love of fellow believers (Romans 12:10; 1 Thessalonians 4:9; 1 Peter 1:22). 'Remain' (menetō) suggests it was already there (6:10; 10:33-34) and must not fade. Chapter 13 turns from argument to practice, and some have wondered whether it was written separately; most readers find its language tied to the rest (13:10-14 continues chapters 9-10).

a: some people have had angels as guests without knowing it
p: Abraham, Lot, Gideon and Manoah all welcomed visitors who turned out to be angels.
b: Abraham ran to meet "three men standing near him" (Genesis 18:2); Lot took in two angels at Sodom (Genesis 19:1-3); Manoah "did not know that this was the angel of the LORD" (Judges 13:16). In Tobit, the angel Raphael travels as a hired guide: "Tobias had no idea that this was an angel of God" (Tobit 5:4); Tobit is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians. Hospitality to strangers was a sacred duty in the ancient world, and traveling Christians depended on it. Jesus: "When I was a stranger, you took me in" (Matthew 25:35).
orig: ἔλαθόν τινες ξενίσαντες ἀγγέλους (elathon tines xenisantes angelous)
r: Genesis 18:1-8; Genesis 19:1-3; Judges 6:11-24; Judges 13:15-21; Tobit 5:4; Matthew 25:35; Romans 12:13

a: since you too live in a body
p: Literally 'being yourselves in a body': you too can suffer, so feel what they feel.
b: The phrase may mean simply 'since you also have bodies that can be hurt', or 'since you too are in the body of Christ' with them. The first is the plainer sense. The readers had already shown this sympathy (10:34).
orig: ὡς καὶ αὐτοὶ ὄντες ἐν σώματι (hōs kai autoi ontes en sōmati)

a: Marriage is to be valued by all
p: A command or a statement? 'Marriage is honorable' (KJV), or 'let marriage be held in honor'.
b: The Greek has no verb: 'honorable the marriage in all'. The KJV reads a statement ('Marriage is honourable in all'), which readers have set against teachers who forbade marriage (1 Timothy 4:3). Most modern readers take it as a command, as the Plain English Translation does. 'In all' may mean 'by everyone' or 'in every way'. The verse holds marriage in honor and sex within it pure; it does not rank marriage against celibacy, which Hebrews does not discuss.
orig: τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν (timios ho gamos en pasin)

a: "I will never let you down, and I will never abandon you."
p: A promise given to Israel through Moses and to Joshua, in a strong form with double negatives.
b: Moses told Israel: "He will not let you down, and he will not abandon you" (Deuteronomy 31:6), and God told Joshua: "I will not let you down, and I will not abandon you" (Joshua 1:5). Hebrews' form, with ou mē twice and in the first person, does not match any one verse exactly; the writer may be quoting freely, or using a form known in worship. The promise is set against love of money: God's presence is better security than wealth.
orig: Οὐ μή σε ἀνῶ οὐδ' οὐ μή σε ἐγκαταλίπω

a: "The Lord is the one who helps me, and I will not be afraid. What can a human being do to me?"
p: The words follow Swete's Septuagint of Psalm 118:6 exactly.
b: The site renders the Hebrew: "With the LORD for me, I have no fear. / What can a human being do to me?" (Psalm 118:6). Swete's Septuagint (Psalm 117:6 in the Greek numbering) reads 'The Lord is my helper', and Hebrews quotes it word for word. Psalm 118 was sung at the great feasts, and the New Testament uses it often (Mark 11:9; Mark 12:10-11).

a: Call to mind your leaders
p: Hēgoumenoi: 'those who lead'. In 13:7 they have died; in 13:17 and 13:24 they are living.
b: Hebrews does not use 'elders' or 'overseers' but the general word hēgoumenoi, 'leaders' (13:7, 17, 24). The first leaders, who preached to them, have died, perhaps as martyrs ('how their way of living ended'). The church is to imitate their faith, as chapter 11 asks of the older heroes. 13:17 turns to their present leaders, and 13:24 sends greetings to them, which suggests the letter went to one group within a larger church.

a: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and for all the ages
t: The same yesterday, today and forever
p: A short confession, perhaps a saying the church already used. What does 'the same' mean?
b: In context, the leaders have died but the one they preached has not changed, so the readers should not be carried off by new teachings (13:9). Christian theology has also cited the verse for Christ's divine unchangeableness, linking it to 1:12, where Psalm 102 says to the Son, 'you are the same'. Readers differ on whether 'yesterday' means his earthly life and the readers' past, or eternity before creation.

a: not by foods
p: The writer warns against teachings about foods. Jewish food laws, sacrificial meals, or something else?
b: Readings: (1) The food laws of the Torah, which some were urging on the readers (compare 9:10, 'only about food and drink'). (2) Meals tied to the Temple's sacrifices or to Jewish festival meals that gave a sense of belonging. (3) Teachings that holiness comes through what one eats or does not eat, of the kind Paul resists (Colossians 2:16, 21; Romans 14:17). The answer in all three: the heart is made firm by grace. 13:10 continues the thought with 'an altar' Christians eat from.

a: We have an altar
t: 'We have an altar': the cross, Christ, or the Lord's Table?
p: One of the most debated verses in Hebrews. Who are 'the people who worship in the tent', and what is the altar?
b: Readings of the altar: (1) the cross, where Christ was offered; (2) Christ himself, offering and altar together; Calvin wrote that "the word altar includes sacrificing and the victim" and read the verse of Christ, with no reference to the Mass; (3) the Eucharist, the Lord's Table, from which believers 'eat'. The Catholic Catechism cites the verse when it says 'The altar of the New Covenant is the Lord's Cross', and goes on: on the church's altar 'the sacrifice of the Cross is made present under sacramental signs', and 'the altar is also the table of the Lord' (paragraph 1182). Who 'has no right to eat': priests of the old tent could not eat the Day of Atonement sin offering, whose body was burned (13:11; Leviticus 6:30); so those who keep to the old system cannot share in Christ, the sin offering. The writer's own next sentences point to the cross 'outside the gate'.

a: their bodies are burned up outside the camp
p: The Day of Atonement sin offerings were not eaten but burned outside the camp.
b: "The bull and the goat for the sin offerings, whose blood was brought in to make atonement in the holy place, are to be taken outside the camp. Their hides, their meat and their dung are to be burned with fire" (Leviticus 16:27). The rule that such offerings were not eaten is in Leviticus 6:30. Hebrews sees in it a picture: the true sin offering is found outside the camp.

a: suffered outside the gate
p: Jesus was crucified outside Jerusalem's walls, as the Gospels say.
b: John says Jesus "went out carrying the cross for himself" and that "the spot where they crucified Jesus was close to the city" (John 19:17, 20). Executions took place outside the city, as the Law required for the stoning of offenders 'outside the camp' (Leviticus 24:14; Numbers 15:35-36). For Hebrews, being outside meant shame and exclusion from the holy place; the writer turns it into the place where holiness is given.
r: John 19:17, 20; Matthew 27:32-33; Mark 15:20; Leviticus 24:14; Numbers 15:35-36; Acts 7:58

a: let us go out to him, outside the camp
p: What were the readers to leave? Judaism and its Temple, the city's safety, or this world?
b: Readings: (1) The readers, Jewish believers, must leave the shelter of the synagogue and Temple worship and accept being outsiders. (2) They must accept social shame and exclusion from the city, the 'camp' of respectable society, for Christ's sake. Calvin wrote: "we must go after him through exiles, flights, reproaches, and all kinds of afflictions." (3) The next verse widens it: no city here lasts. Readers today note that 'outside the camp' was the place of the unclean (Leviticus 13:46) and of the tent of meeting in Exodus 33:7.

a: a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess his name
p: Psalms and Hosea already spoke of praise as a sacrifice and of 'the fruit of lips'.
b: The Septuagint of Psalm 50:14 (Swete's edition, mainly Codex Vaticanus; 49:14 in the Greek numbering) reads 'sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise' (thysian aineseōs); the site's Hebrew has "Sacrifice a thank offering to God" (Psalm 50:14). The Greek of Hosea 14:2 (14:3 in Swete) has 'we will repay the fruit of our lips', where the site's Hebrew has "let us pay you the bulls of our lips" (Hosea 14:2). The Talmud records the view of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the daily prayers 'were instituted based on the daily offerings' (Berakhot 26b). Hebrews' 'sacrifices' are praise and doing good (13:16).
r: Psalm 50:14, 23; Hosea 14:2; Psalm 107:22; Psalm 116:17; Romans 12:1; 1 Peter 2:5

a: kindness and sharing
p: Koinōnia here means sharing goods, the practical side of fellowship.
b: Koinōnia often means fellowship; here, with 'doing good' (eupoiia), it means sharing possessions with those in need, as in Romans 15:26 and 2 Corinthians 9:13. Paul calls the Philippians' gift "a sacrifice that God accepts and that pleases him" (Philippians 4:18).
orig: τῆς δὲ εὐποιΐας καὶ κοινωνίας (tēs de eupoiias kai koinōnias)

a: Listen to your leaders and yield to them
p: How far does the duty to obey church leaders reach? The verse is read through each church's order.
b: Peithesthe means 'be persuaded by, obey'; hypeikete means 'give way, yield'. The leaders are not named by office. Churches with bishops and priests read the verse of their ordained ministers; congregational churches read it of elected elders and pastors, accountable to the church. All read the limit in the verse itself: leaders 'must give an account' to God. The tone is pastoral: make their work a joy, not a groan.
orig: Πείθεσθε τοῖς ἡγουμένοις ὑμῶν καὶ ὑπείκετε

a: so that I may be returned to you soon
p: The writer is kept from them, perhaps by prison, illness or work, and hopes to be restored to them.
b: 'Returned' (apokatastathō) means restored. The writer knew this congregation and had been with them. The letter does not say what prevents his return. Along with 'I' in 11:32 and 13:22-23, this is one of the few personal notes in a book that never names its author.

a: the great shepherd of the sheep
t: Brought up from the dead: the great shepherd
p: The words echo Isaiah 63:11 as Swete's Septuagint has it, where God brought Moses, the shepherd, up out of the sea.
b: Swete's Septuagint of Isaiah 63:11 asks: 'Where is the one who brought up from the sea the shepherd of the sheep?' (ho anabibasas ek tēs thalassēs ton poimena tōn probatōn). The site's Hebrew: "Where is the one who brought them up out of the sea / with the shepherds of his flock?" (Isaiah 63:11). Hebrews moves the image from the sea to death: God 'led up out of the dead' the great shepherd. This is the only direct mention of Jesus' resurrection in Hebrews. 'The blood of an eternal covenant' may echo Zechariah 9:11, "because of the blood of your covenant" (Zechariah 9:11).
r: Isaiah 63:11; Zechariah 9:11; Ezekiel 37:26; John 10:11; 1 Peter 2:25; 1 Peter 5:4

a: To him be glory
p: 'To him' may be God, the subject of the blessing, or Jesus Christ, the nearest name.
b: Greek relative pronouns usually refer to the nearest noun, here 'Jesus Christ'; but the whole prayer is addressed to 'the God of peace'. If to Christ, it is one of the doxologies in the New Testament that give glory directly to Jesus (2 Peter 3:18; Revelation 1:5-6). 'Forever and ever' is literally 'to the ages of the ages'; the SBL edition has only 'to the ages'.
orig: ᾧ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας (hō hē doxa eis tous aiōnas)

a: word of exhortation
t: A word of exhortation: a sermon
p: The same phrase names a synagogue sermon in Acts 13:15. Hebrews calls itself a sermon.
b: In Pisidian Antioch the synagogue leaders said to Paul and his companions: "Brothers, if any of you has a word to encourage the people, speak up" (Acts 13:15). The Greek there is logos paraklēseōs, the phrase used here. Hebrews reads like a sermon: it says 'we are speaking' (2:5; 5:11; 6:9), and moves between explaining Scripture and urging the hearers. 'A short letter' may be a polite remark.
orig: τοῦ λόγου τῆς παρακλήσεως (tou logou tēs paraklēseōs)

a: our brother Timothy has been released
p: Timothy, Paul's coworker, had been in prison or under arrest. The writer belongs to Paul's circle.
b: Timothy joined Paul at Lystra (Acts 16:1-3) and is named in many of Paul's letters. The mention places the writer among Paul's companions, which is one reason Paul himself was long thought to be the author; it fits Apollos, Barnabas, Luke, Silas or Priscilla as well. 'Released' (apolelymenon) usually means set free from custody, but can mean 'sent off' on a journey.

a: The people from Italy greet you
p: Italians away from home sending greetings to Rome, or Christians in Italy greeting a church elsewhere?
b: Hoi apo tēs Italias can mean 'those who are in Italy' or 'those who have come from Italy'. (1) If the writer is outside Italy, Italian believers with him send greetings home: the letter went to Rome. Acts tells of Priscilla and Aquila, who "had just come from Italy" (Acts 18:2). (2) If the writer is in Italy, the greeting goes from Italian Christians to a church elsewhere: Jerusalem, Alexandria, Antioch and others have been proposed. Many modern scholars favor Rome. The later subscription 'written from Italy' took the second view (see the variant at 13:25).
orig: οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰταλίας (hoi apo tēs Italias)
